transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-22 16:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Martello - Head of Platform), Ethan Cole (Martello CTO), Samir Patel (Martello SRE lead)

Auto-summary (auto):
- Primary goal: understand per-token economics and whether Martello should start hosted pilot or plan for dedicated/residency later.
- Key constraints: strict budget ceilings for Q3 POC, SOC2 required, possible on-prem later for regulated flows, p95 latency target ~220ms for 512-token average responses.
- Next steps: pricing sheet + cost model, SE deep-dive, run 2-week pilot with sampled prompts, share security package.

Topics: per-token pricing, batching and KV cache impact, hosted vs dedicated vs private residency, SOC2/KMS, pilot scope and timelines

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account, with Diego our solutions engineer. How are you all?
[00:08] Priya Nair: Hi Maya, hi Diego, doing well. We appreciate you fitting us in. Quick call, we're trying to decide how to get rolling without blowing the Q3 budget.
[00:17] Diego Alvarez: Great, good to meet you. We'll keep this pragmatic — focus on pricing levers and what a minimal pilot looks like.
[00:22] Ethan Cole: If possible can we start with per-token so we can map to product metrics. We have two major flows: a 120-token user query with short answer (avg response 80-150 tokens) and a 600-token summary job batched overnight.
[00:36] Samir Patel: And we have a regulatory route that needs residency eventually, so private or on-prem could be on the table. For the pilot though, hosted is easier.
[00:45] Maya Chen: Totally. Quick framing: our hosted API has straightforward per-token rates and is the lowest-friction. Dedicated gives committed capacity and lower unit costs at higher commit levels. Private/on-prem is available but adds setup time and licensing. The main levers that reduce per-token cost are batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantized model variants.
[01:10] Priya Nair: Can you explain the batching effect? We have bursty interactive traffic but also those overnight summarizations.
[01:17] Diego Alvarez: Sure — batching groups tokens across concurrent requests to amortize fixed kernel work. For streaming/interactive, continuous batching gives wins when you have many concurrent short queries. For the overnight job you can put huge batches to maximize throughput. Realistic delta: batching can shave 10-60% depending on concurrency and sequence lengths. Also prefix/KV cache helps if you have repeated context like templates, which reduces decoder work per request.
[01:45] Ethan Cole: When you say 10-60% that's pretty wide — what's typical for a company our size? We do maybe 6-12 qps during peak for interactive flow.
[01:55] Diego Alvarez: At 6-12 qps, interactive batching alone might be in the 12-25% savings range for a 120-token average, but if you enable KV cache (we cache common system prompts & user metadata) you could see closer to 30-40% on those repeated prompt patterns. The overnight 600-token jobs — if you can queue them and let them run in dedicated batches — can hit the higher end, 50%+.
[02:20] Priya Nair: And dedicated vs hosted unit cost? We have a pretty tight budget: cap at $X/month (Priya blurts the actual number, but it's redacted in notes).
[02:30] Maya Chen: Without quoting exact numbers here, hosted is pay-as-you-go with a unit price; dedicated is a reserved pool where per-token can be materially lower if you commit. Important to model your mix: if interactive is 70% of tokens and batch 30%, we can show whether a dedicated commit pays back in 3-6 months.
[02:49] Samir Patel: What about model variants — do you support quantized models that reduce cost but affect latency or quality?
[02:56] Diego Alvarez: Yes. We have quantization profiles: int8/quantized weights that lower GPU memory and cost. The runtime picks kernels for latency-sensitive paths. Typically quality impact is minimal for retrieval-augmented prompts and simple summarization, but for highly sensitive legal text you might want FP16/FP32. We also can route sensitive flows to higher-fidelity variants.
[03:20] Ethan Cole: For the residency use-case, what's the rough time to spin up private deployment? We're not ready to go on-prem immediately but want the option.
[03:29] Maya Chen: Private deployments (VPC) usually take 4-6 weeks for most customers, on-prem longer and requires packaging and audits. We'll surface the dependencies — certs, network peering, KMS integration — in the deck we'll send.
[03:40] Priya Nair: Security is a gating factor. SOC 2 is a must, and we have to prove audit logs retention and key management.
[03:46] Maya Chen: We can share our SOC 2 and ISO docs; we also support customer-managed keys (KMS) and HSM integrations for private installs.
[03:56] Diego Alvarez: Also worth calling out: audit log granularity — in hosted we capture per-request metadata for 90 days by default and longer retention is an add-on. For private, you manage retention and export.
[04:10] Samir Patel: Back to economics — can you walk through a simple per-call example? Say a 120-token request with 40 tokens prompt and 80 tokens generated.
[04:19] Diego Alvarez: Sure. Baseline per-token multiply + model overhead. Example: if baseline per-token price is P_hosted, the effective cost per call = prompt_tokens*P + generated_tokens*P minus batching savings and cache savings. So if P=0.0009 for hosted and you get 25% effective savings from batching+cache, your effective call cost drops proportionally. We'll run the numbers for your exact traffic in the model.
[04:46] Ethan Cole: Could you show an example with the overnight summary? If we batch the 600-token job, what's changed?
[04:54] Diego Alvarez: For large jobs the amortized overhead is small so effective per-token is closer to kernel throughput. In dedicated pools, we can tune kernel selection for long seqs and get 30-60% improvement over naive hosted throughput.
[05:10] Priya Nair: I want to understand the break-even for dedicated. What inputs should we give you?
[05:17] Maya Chen: Provide: monthly token volume per flow, concurrency distribution, p95 latency targets, and what percent of traffic needs residency. With those we can model commit size and payback period.
[05:29] Ethan Cole: We'll have that. Two more questions — routing/fallbacks and throttling. If hosted capacity is constrained, do you fallback to smaller models?
[05:38] Diego Alvarez: Yes our smart routing can downgrade to compatible model variants or region fallback per policy. You can set routing rules by latency or cost thresholds. That helps keep SLAs without committing immediately.
[05:50] Samir Patel: Is there a risk of quality regression with those fallbacks in sensitive flows?
[05:55] Diego Alvarez: There's always tradeoff. For mission-critical flows we recommend pinning to a production model and using canaries. For non-critical features price-first fallbacks can be acceptable. Redwood's console surfaces quality regressions and we can tie alerts to eval prompts you provide.
[06:12] Priya Nair: About the pilot: our procurement window opens mid-June — can we do a two-week pilot in early June?
[06:20] Maya Chen: Early June sounds doable. Typical pilot: 2 weeks with a scoped token cap and defined SLAs; we instrument tracing and cost telemetry so you can inspect per-route token breakdown.
[06:30] Ethan Cole: For the pilot, will you provision a dedicated small pool or is it hosted?
[06:35] Maya Chen: Pilots are often hosted to reduce lead time; however, we can do a short dedicated trial if you commit to a short reserved capacity — depends on your willingness to sign a small commitment. We can show both scenarios in the pricing sheet.
[06:49] Samir Patel: We need to understand token inflation from prompt engineering we plan to do. If we change prompts mid-pilot, how will that affect economics?
[06:58] Diego Alvarez: We'll help run sensitivity analysis. The console lets you compare before/after prompt sets and shows token deltas. For planning assume a 10-30% variance depending on complexity.
[07:12] Priya Nair: One item — we use internal embeddings for reranking and then call the LLM; embeddings cost separate, right?
[07:18] Diego Alvarez: Correct, embeddings are billed differently; in the model we'll include both embedding and generation costs. Often you can cache embeddings and reduce calls which helps.
[07:27] Ethan Cole: For billing — invoices and usage reporting — can we get daily CSV exports?
[07:32] Maya Chen: Yes, hosted can push daily usage exports to an S3 bucket or via API. Dedicated has more granular telemetry as well.
[07:40] Priya Nair: Do you have an example cost model for a company that had 40M tokens/month and mixed traffic?
[07:46] Maya Chen: We do — Diego, remember that one from last quarter?
[07:49] Diego Alvarez: Yup, a media customer. We'll include a sample model but we'll recalibrate to your traffic. That case showed dedicated made sense at ~120M tokens/month due to commit discounts and static baseline.
[08:02] Ethan Cole: Any gotchas with KV cache in multi-tenant setups — we'll have multiple product lines under one account.
[08:10] Diego Alvarez: KV cache is per model instance; in multi-tenant you can set tenant-level keys or segregated model instances. There's a small memory tradeoff but better hit rates if you group similar tenants. We can recommend a partitioning strategy.
[08:24] Samir Patel: About latency: our p95 target is ~220ms for the 120-token interactive path. Will hosted meet that consistently?
[08:32] Diego Alvarez: Hosted across our primary region can meet that for most runs; p95 depends heavily on sequence length and concurrency. For strong p95 guarantees we often recommend dedicated or dedicated+burst which gives you predictable tail latency.
[08:47] Priya Nair: Procurement — what paperwork is typical for a pilot? We'll need an MSA and DPA.
[08:54] Maya Chen: We'll share a standard pilot agreement, MSA, and DPA. For enterprise terms we can route to legal but pilot paperwork is lightweight.
[09:03] Ethan Cole: Are there volume discounts or caps we can lock in?
[09:08] Maya Chen: Yes, volume tiers and commit discounts are part of Dedicated and Enterprise. For hosted we can offer a pilot discount. We'll capture the ask in the pricing sheet.
[09:16] Priya Nair: Let's talk about timeline: if we go hosted pilot in early June, what do you need from us this week?
[09:23] Maya Chen: If you can share traffic slices (sample logs or estimated token distribution), desired pilot flows, and the compliance contacts, we'll prepare pricing and SE benchmark plan.
[09:33] Priya Nair: I'll send that by Tuesday.
[09:36] Maya Chen: Perfect. Diego, anything to add on benchmarks?
[09:39] Diego Alvarez: We'll request a small prompt set (50-100 representative prompts) and a sample of your concurrency profile. We'll then run latency/throughput tests and a token economics sheet showing hosted vs dedicated vs private projections.
[09:56] Ethan Cole: About quality monitoring — you mentioned evals earlier — can we set baseline metrics?
[10:03] Diego Alvarez: Absolutely. Redwood Optimize ties evals to rollouts; we can run automated prompts and flag quality regressions during a rollout or when you change prompt templates. We'll include that in the pilot instrumentation.
[10:17] Samir Patel: One more operational question — how do we handle secrets and keys in hosted vs private?
[10:23] Maya Chen: Hosted supports envelope encryption and you can bring your own key (BYOK) in many cases; private gives you full KMS control. We'll document options in the security packet.
[10:33] Priya Nair: Excellent. Any other blockers?
[10:35] Ethan Cole: I think cost mapping and a concrete pilot scope are all we need to decide.
[10:40] Maya Chen: Great, recap: Maya sends pricing + pilot options, Diego sends benchmark plan, Priya shares traffic profile and compliance contacts. We'll target a pilot start in early June.
[10:53] Priya Nair: Sounds good. Thanks folks.
[10:56] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the materials today.

End of call.

Notes about transcription quirks: occasional speaker overlap, some product names were auto-transcribed (e.g., KV cache sometimes shown as K V cache, on-prem spelled on perm), numeric values redacted in this export.
